node-1.label: A 72-year-old woman experienced behavioural changes, unsteadiness, and frequent falls over the past year

node-2.label: Over the past year, relatives reported that she became listless, neglected work and domestic activities, exhibited hyperreligious behaviour, anxiety, loss of appetite, mild lower limb weakness, and falls; later she had episodes of agitation, confusion, and visual hallucinations, leading to initiation of antipsychotic medication, and eventually lost the ability to walk and became wheelchair-bound

node-3.label: On admission, she showed disorientation, apathy, apraxia, short-term memory deficit (MMSE = 7), anosmia, mild flaccid proximal paraparesis, and muscular atrophy; patellar reflexes and plantar responses were normal; urinary incontinence was present without signs of sensory impairment

node-4.label: She had started oral anticoagulant therapy two years earlier due to paroxysmal atrial fibrillation; 24-hour Holter monitoring revealed no paroxysmal atrial fibrillation

node-5.label: A comprehensive workup including vitamin levels, thyroid function, tumour markers, full-body CT, and breast ultrasound was unremarkable; EEG indicated diffuse cerebral dysfunction without epileptic activity

attrs.why: New MRI evidence shows cortical and brainstem T2* hypointensities suggesting iron deposition, and expert analyses note that frontotemporal dementia lacks confirmatory frontotemporal atrophy or FDG-PET hypometabolism. Although behavioral changes, apraxia, anosmia, and memory loss keep frontotemporal dementia the most credible hypothesis, the absence of definitive supportive imaging and the presence of an alternative MRI finding lower confidence from 0.65 to 0.55.

Expert laboratory analysis and prior Holter/anticoagulation indicate vascular etiologies are basically excluded. The MRI T2* signal could suggest vascular factors but is nonspecific and not sufficient to support active vascular cognitive impairment. Confidence decreases from 0.2 to 0.1.

Expert analyses maintain that normal pressure hydrocephalus remains possible and is not excluded, as current MRI did not provide Evans index/DESH. With vascular and metabolic alternatives further excluded, the relative likelihood of normal pressure hydrocephalus increases slightly from 0.15 to 0.2.
Expert analyses and the comprehensive negative systemic workup effectively exclude metabolic/toxic encephalopathy. Confidence decreases from 0.05 to 0.02.

The current frontier 'Neurodegenerative disease (FTD)' is still a broad category and can be refined. The predominant, early behavioral/personality change (listlessness, neglect of work, hyperreligiosity, agitation, confusion) coupled with apraxia, anosmia and a markedly reduced MMSE (7) but no aphasia (graph nodes node-2 and node-3, both supporting node-6) is the classic presentation of the behavioral variant, the most common FTD subtype; thus bvFTD is the most parsimonious refinement of the frontier.

node-14.label: Frontotemporal dementia with motor neuron disease (FTD-MND/FTD-ALS)

attrs.why: Refines the frontier by linking the mild flaccid proximal paraparesis and muscular atrophy with preserved patellar/plantar responses (node-3) to the neurodegenerative process. FTD-MND is a recognized FTD subtype and would explain these otherwise atypical lower-motor-neuron signs accompanying the frontotemporal syndrome, a next-level distinction not captured by the umbrella node.

A related FTD-spectrum tauopathy that further refines the frontier; the prominent apraxia and progressive gait/limb weakness progressing to wheelchair dependence (node-2, node-3) make this a plausible though less common specific neurodegenerative alternative, justifying it as a finer-grained hypothesis beneath the current FTD node.
